newsitem.title: CONGO: Fighting eases as population flees Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Fighting eases as population flees Brazzaville.

text.p: Thousands of civilians have poured out of Brazzaville, fleeing the heaviest fighting in a three-week-old war.

At least 17,000 people have fled from the inner suburbs of Congo's capital since a merciless battle for the airport erupted on Wednesday between pro- and anti-presidential factions, an international Red Cross (ICRC) spokesman said.
The fighting raged for most of Thursday but subsided overnight. No shelling was heard on Friday morning.
But there were was a fresh eruption of the street battles which have steadily approached the French embassy in the paralysed and deserted city centre.

French ambassador Raymond Cesaire, the last foreign envoy in Brazzaville, was deciding on Friday whether to pull out with his 30-odd staff and gendarmes to the relative safety of his residence in the southern suburbs.
Hopes that a planned U.N. peacekeeping force could come swiftly to shore up a ceasefire have faded along with the truce.
The remaining foreign Red Cross staff pulled out by boat from the former French colonial capital to Kinshasa, across the Congo river in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
"They have all left," ICRC spokesman Paolo dell'Oca said.
The city they left behind had been plunged deeper into chaos with the artillery battle for Maya-Maya airport.

An estimated 1,000-3,000 people have already died in the clashes between the forces of President Pascal Lissouba, a former plant geneticist, and his enemy Denis Sassou Nguesso, Congo's Marxist leader for 13 years.
The two were rivals for presidential elections due in a month's time.
The Bacongo suburb, once a haven of peace held by neutral city mayor Bernard Kolelas, has been hit by dozens of shells.
Several landed in the maternity ward of a hospital on Wednesday, killing a woman who was giving birth.
"We don't know how many wounded there are. The staff, the patients, everyone fled," hospital spokesman Faustin Missakila said, standing amid the shattered buildings.
Despite the shelling, Kolelas hosted fresh mediation talks but without clear progress.
A week-long ceasefire he brokered took some sting out of the battles and let 1,250 French soldiers leave peacefully after evacuating foreigners. But the truce then collapsed.
Losing Maya-Maya, about five km from the dissected city centre, would be a big blow to Lissouba.
Both sides claimed control of the airport but there was no independent confirmation.
Sassou's aides claimed Lissouba was bringing in Liberian and Angolan UNITA mercenaries to help fight back.
